route: The strategy-evaluation oracle model: query complexity of the sink on orientations SSGs realise
object: The deterministic query complexity of SSG-Value in an oracle model whose unit of cost is one strategy evaluation, together with a new invariant of a stopping game — its evaluation dimension d(G), the affine dimension of the set {val_sigma restricted to C} — which bounds that complexity from above, and an explicit family that bounds it from below.
headline: The evaluation-query complexity of a stopping SSG is Theta(|C|): at most d(G)+2 <= |C|+2 evaluations of Max strategies always suffice (an explicit algorithm, correct with a certificate, verified on games up to 344 vertices and on 300 random instances), and |Vmax| are necessary on an explicit one-player family HDP_m on 6m vertices; consequently NO adversary argument in this model can prove a lower bound above |C|+2, every exponential lower bound in the paper (thm:ladder, cor:slack-stalls, thm:wedge-proved, thm:hybrid-lower, thm:cv-lower) and any future exponential bottom-antipodal-height family is a bound on the ROUNDS of a fixed rule and not on the information a rule collects — on the ladder's least-index run of 64 strategies only 7 rounds carry any information at all, the other 57 being predicted exactly, values and appeals, by every game consistent with what came before.

results.name: Evaluation is cheap: at most d(G)+2 <= |C|+2 strategy evaluations
results.statement: Let G be a stopping SSG with C = Vmax u Vmin and evaluation dimension d(G) := dim aff{val_sigma|_C : sigma in {0,1}^Vmax} <= |C|. Consider the model in which an algorithm is given only the controlled skeleton Sigma(G) = (C, the owner of each v in C, the names of its two successors with their coincidences and which are sinks) — nothing whatever about Vavg — and may query sigma to receive val_sigma at C and at the successors of C. Then there is a deterministic algorithm (Algorithm E) that outputs an optimal Max strategy, together with a checkable certificate of optimality, after at most d(G)+2 <= |C|+2 <= N queries. The same bound and the same proof hold for the profile oracle, which takes a positional PAIR and returns val_{sigma,tau}.
results.why_not_implied: thm:compare-equivalence counts calls to SSG-Compare, an oracle for the problem itself, so its n non-adaptive calls carry no information content and bound nothing about polynomial-time strategy evaluations; nothing in the paper bounds the number of val_sigma computations an algorithm needs, and the bound here comes from a rank argument on the harmonic normal form, not from a reduction (thm:order-determines is likewise about a certificate for w*, not about adaptive evaluations).
results.argument:
ALGORITHM E. Keep the list D of answers, an answer being (x,A) with x = val_sigma|_C and A(v,a) = val_sigma(v^(a)). Choose any HARMONIC SYSTEM rho-hat on Sigma(G) consistent with D — rows (q_{v,a}, p_{v,a}) >= 0 with q + |p|_1 <= 1, no nonempty U <= C in which every vertex has a full-mass action supported in U, and q-hat_{v,a} + p-hat_{v,a}.x = A(v,a) for every recorded (x,A). Let w-hat be the fixed point of T_{rho-hat} and sigma-hat Max-greedy at w-hat; query sigma-hat; halt and output it if the answer has S_{sigma-hat} = empty, else append and repeat.

LEMMA (harmonic form). For stopping G let rho_{v,a} be the first-passage law of action a at v onto C u {t1} (the harmonic normal form already used at lem:rise-bound and thm:lasserre-vacuous). (a) rho is a harmonic system: absorption into C u {t0,t1} is a.s. because a trajectory staying in Vavg for ever never reaches a sink; and a nonempty full-mass U would, together with the average vertices strictly between, be a nonempty trap, against lem:trapchar. (b) If y in [0,1]^V is the mean of its successors at every average vertex with y(t0)=0, y(t1)=1, then y(v^(a)) = q_{v,a} + p_{v,a}.y|_C — optional stopping at the hitting time of C u {t0,t1} for the bounded martingale y(X_k); in particular val_{sigma,tau}|_C, val_sigma|_C and w*|_C are fixed points of the corresponding operators. (c) Every operator of a harmonic system has exactly one fixed point: with (S xi)_v := max_a p_{v,a}.xi, S^n 1 decreases to a fixed point xi, and max xi > 0 would force a full-mass set (p.xi = mu with xi <= mu and p >= 0 forces |p|_1 = 1, hence q = 0, and equality forces supp p inside {xi = mu}); so S^n 1 -> 0, ||S^n 1|| <= 1/2 for some n, and |T^n y - T^n y'| <= S^n|y-y'| pointwise since |opt_a A_a - opt_a B_a| <= max_a |A_a - B_a|. This is exactly the argument of lem:survival-contract, which the paper states for an arbitrary finite family of substochastic first-passage rows over C.

WELL DEFINED: rho_G is consistent with D at every stage, so the choice set is nonempty; w-hat is unique by (c), and T_{rho-hat,sigma-hat} w-hat = w-hat, so w-hat is the hypothesis's value of sigma-hat and no Max vertex is switchable there for the hypothesis.
CORRECT: the halting test reads true values, so lem:local-global gives val_{sigma-hat} = w*.
TERMINATION: put u(x) := (1,x) in R^{1+C} and V_t := span{u(x) : (x,A) in D} after t answers. Consistency says precisely rho-hat_{v,a} - rho_{G,v,a} is orthogonal to V_t for every (v,a). Suppose the (t+1)-st query does not halt and let x = val_{sigma-hat}|_C. If u(x) were in V_t then q-hat + p-hat.x = q + p.x = val_{sigma-hat}(v^(a)) for EVERY (v,a) by (b); taking the frozen/optimised choice at each controlled vertex makes x a fixed point of T_{rho-hat,sigma-hat}, hence by (c) THE hypothesis value of sigma-hat, and the same identity makes the hypothesis's appeals at sigma-hat the true ones — so the hypothesis's switchable set, empty by construction, is the true one and the query halts, a contradiction. Hence u(x) is not in V_t and dim V grows by exactly one at every non-halting query. Since dim V_0 = 0 and every recorded x lies in the value set, whose affine hull has dimension d(G), there are at most d(G)+1 non-halting queries and at most d(G)+2 in all.
PROFILE ORACLE: replace sigma-hat by a greedy PAIR at w-hat; the halting test asks that no controlled vertex be strictly switchable, which by (b) makes val_{sigma,tau} a fixed point of the Shapley operator, hence w* by thm:contraction; the rank argument is unchanged.
Note the proof uses no property of the selection of rho-hat beyond consistency and the stopping condition, and that the step it cannot do in polynomial time is solving the hypothesis, itself an SSG-valued problem on the same controlled set.
results.verification: Algorithm E implemented in exact rational arithmetic (code_dir/qm.py): harmonic() computes the first-passage rows by an exact linear solve — checked against the paper's printed harmonic normal form of W_10 in thm:lasserre-vacuous, reproduced exactly; choose_hypothesis() picks a consistent harmonic system by one small exact simplex per row (least p-mass, then greatest q) with a repair loop pinning a vertex's rows to escape-maximisers when the greedy choice has a nonempty full-mass trap; the oracle takes val_sigma as the componentwise minimum over ALL positional tau of exact profile values, never by greedy iteration. The assertion rank(V_{t+1}) = rank(V_t)+1 at every non-halting query is checked inside the loop and never fired. Query counts, output always verified equal to a brute-force w*, all within |C|+2: G8 2, S 1, S_r(1..4) 2, H_2..H_5 1, G* 2, WD(2,2,4)/(2,3,5)/(3,4,7) 1, CC(2,3)/(6,7)/(10,11) 1, CV(1,4)/(3,4)/(5,4) 1, L_2 3, L_4 5, L_6 7, L_8 8, RC(2)/(5)/(8) 1, B1_game (56 vertices) 1, B2_small_GAME (136 vertices, |C|=6) 5, H5_GAME (344 vertices, |C|=5) 4, TB_GAME_D10 (192 vertices, |C|=8) 5; plus 300 random two-player stopping games with |C| up to 9 (all correct, all within |C|+2, worst q-|C| = 1). d(G) computed exactly for the same games: q <= d(G)+2 in every case, with d(G) = |C| for the ladders, HDP, RC, B2_small, H5, TB_D10, d = 4 < 7 = |C| for G*, d = 1 for CV(e,s). An earlier selection rule (least p-mass alone) attained d+2 = 7 on H5_GAME, so the bound is attained by some instantiation. The profile-oracle variant learn_profile was run on L_3, L_6, G*, B1 and 120 random games: correct and within |C|+2 throughout. Logs: verify_all.log, dimrun.log, namedrun.log.

results.name: Evaluation is not free: the hidden decision path HDP_m needs |Vmax| queries
results.statement: For m >= 1 and z in {0,1}^m let HDP_m(z) be the one-player stopping SSG on 6m non-sink vertices in which v_j points at two private average successors e^j_0, e^j_1 (the same names for every z); the one indexed z_j leads to a gadget of value 1/2 (j=1) or to a gadget whose first-passage law onto C u {t1} is (1/8 ; (1/2) e_{v_{j-1}}) (j >= 2), the other to a gadget of value 1/4. All 2^m members have the same controlled skeleton and Opt(HDP_m(z)) = {z}. Every deterministic evaluation algorithm needs at least m queries on the family, m suffice, and every zero-error randomised one needs at least m/log_2(m+1) queries in expectation on a uniform member. With thm:qm-eval this gives m <= Q <= |C|+2 for one-player stopping SSGs.
results.why_not_implied: thm:ladder lower-bounds the rounds of ONE named rule (least index) on ONE game, and L_n is in fact solved by |C| evaluations, so it yields no lower bound valid against algorithms that may evaluate arbitrary strategies; HDP is a family with a single controlled skeleton whose oracle answers provably reveal one bit of the optimum at a time, which is a statement about all algorithms and has no counterpart in the paper.
results.argument:
Write i(sigma,z) = min{j : sigma_j != z_j} (m+1 if none). Solving x_j = Psi_{j,sigma_j}(x) with Psi_{j,z_j}(x) = 1/8 + x_{j-1}/2 (= 1/2 for j=1) and Psi_{j,1-z_j} = 1/4 gives x_j = 1/4 + 2^{-j-1} for j < i and x_j = 1/4 for j >= i, by induction: a mismatch at j pins x_j = 1/4, and 1/8 + (1/4)/2 = 1/4 propagates the low value upward. Hence the appeals at v_j are (1/4 + 2^{-j-1}, 1/4) for j <= i, with the larger one chosen exactly when j < i — so v_i is the unique strictly switchable vertex — and (1/4, 1/4), a tie, for j > i. Therefore the whole oracle answer (values at C and at the successors of C, indexed by name) is a function of sigma and i alone, and it determines i, hence z_1..z_{i-1} = sigma_1..sigma_{i-1} and z_i = 1-sigma_i, and nothing else. Opt = {z} since S_z is empty and S_sigma is not for sigma != z. Stopping: the trap test of lem:trapchar deletes the gadget tails, then their entries, then every v_j.
UPPER BOUND: query 0^m, then repeatedly the known prefix padded with zeros; each query extends the known prefix by at least one bit, so m queries suffice.
LOWER BOUND (adversary): keep a prefix p, initially empty. On a query sigma set i := min{j <= |p| : sigma_j != p_j} if that set is nonempty, else i := |p|+1 and extend p by 1 - sigma_{|p|+1}; answer with the unique answer belonging to (sigma, i). Every z extending p is consistent with all answers so far, because z_j = p_j for j <= |p| makes i(sigma^s,z) = i_s for each past query. After q queries |p| <= q; if q <= m-1 at least two extensions survive, they have different optima, and any output now is wrong for one of them.
RANDOMISED: fix the random string; the algorithm becomes a deterministic decision tree of branching at most m+1 (the answer is a function of sigma and i in {1..m+1}) which must have at least 2^m leaves, one per z; a tree of branching b with L leaves has average leaf depth at least log_b L, so the expected number of queries under uniform z is at least m/log_2(m+1), and averaging over the random string preserves it.
NOTE (honest scope): the members of the family are pairwise isomorphic, so val(v) is the same number in all of them; the lower bound is for the SEARCH problem (name an optimal strategy), which is what every rule in the paper solves, not for the threshold decision on this family.
results.verification: code_dir/hdp.py builds HDP_m(z) for every z and checks in exact arithmetic, for m = 2,3,4,5: every member stopping by the trap test; all 2^m members have literally identical vertex kinds and an identical successor map on Vmax, i.e. ONE controlled skeleton (printed as 'distinct controlled skeletons: 1'); the value vector equal to 1/4 + 2^{-j-1} for j < i and 1/4 for j >= i at every one of the 2^m strategies; the strictly switchable set exactly {v_i}, empty iff sigma = z, so Opt = {z}; and the full name-indexed oracle answer constant on every class {(sigma,i)} — over all 2^m games times 2^m strategies, 0 of the (sigma,i) buckets held two different answers, which is exactly the consistency the adversary needs. Algorithm E of thm:qm-eval takes between 1 and m+1 queries over the 2^m members (bound m+2). Log: verify_all.log section C.

results.name: No evaluation-model barrier: the paper's exponential lower bounds carry no information
results.statement: For every class of stopping SSGs with |C| <= c the evaluation-query complexity is at most c+2; so no adversary argument in this model can prove more. In particular L_n (thm:ladder), H_m (cor:slack-stalls), WD(e,j,m) (thm:wedge-proved), CC(L,m) (thm:hybrid-lower) and CV(e,s) (thm:cv-lower) — each of which defeats some rule or calculus for 2^{Omega(N)} rounds — are each solved by at most |C|+2 evaluations, and a family of exponential bottom-antipodal height realised on polynomially many vertices (the open programme of rem:blowup-realise) would defeat all-switches without being an informational obstacle: the same instances would be solved by |C|+2 evaluations of the very operation those rules perform once per round. The subexponential bound of thm:subexp is likewise a bound on a rule that follows improving switches and reads only the orientation.
results.why_not_implied: rem:blowup-realise states what a family of exponential height would buy (defeating all-switches and M3); it does not say — and nothing in the paper says — that such a family is solved by linearly many evaluations, which is what limits in advance what the whole blow-up programme can deliver against unrestricted evaluation algorithms.
results.argument: Immediate from thm:qm-eval, whose bound is unconditional over the class; the named families are then instances. The content is the identification of what the paper's negative results do and do not bound: they bound the number of rounds of a rule that must move along improving switches (or must propagate a calculus), never the number of val_sigma computations available to an algorithm free to choose its evaluation points. In particular the passage of prop:allsw-auso from the game to its improvement orientation, which discards the numbers, is where the exponential behaviour lives.
results.verification: Every family in the list was run through Algorithm E in exact arithmetic with the output checked against a brute-force w*: L_2/L_4/L_6/L_8 in 3/5/7/8 queries (|C| = 2/4/6/8), H_2..H_5 in 1, WD(2,2,4)/(2,3,5)/(3,4,7) in 1, CC(2,3)/(6,7)/(10,11) in 1, CV(1,4)/(3,4)/(5,4) in 1, and the largest realisations in the repository — B1_game 1 query, B2_small_GAME (136 vertices) 5, H5_GAME (344 vertices) 4, TB_GAME_D10 (192 vertices) 5. Logs: verify_all.log section A, dimrun.log, namedrun.log.

results.name: A run stops informing after |C|+1 rounds
results.statement: Let sigma^0, sigma^1, ... be any sequence of Max strategies (a run of any rule) in a stopping SSG G, and R_s := span{(1, val_{sigma^r}|_C) : r <= s}. Then (1, val_{sigma^s}|_C) lies outside R_{s-1} for at most d(G)+1 <= |C|+1 indices s, and at every other index BOTH the value restriction val_{sigma^s}|_C and all its appeals val_{sigma^s}(v^(a)) are already determined: every harmonic system consistent with the answers at sigma^0..sigma^{s-1} predicts them exactly. An exponentially long run therefore spends all but at most |C|+1 of its rounds recomputing consequences of what its first few evaluations already implied.
results.why_not_implied: cor:law-u and its companions (cor:no-return, cor:antichain, thm:peak-law) are combinatorial constraints on the SWITCHED SETS of an all-switches run; none of them says anything about the linear algebra of the value vectors, and in particular none implies that all but |C|+1 rounds of a run are exactly predictable from the earlier rounds.
results.argument: The rank of a set of vectors in R^{1+C} is at most d(G)+1 because every (1, val_sigma|_C) lies in the linear span of {(1,y) : y in the value set}, whose dimension is 1 + dim aff of that set; a strictly increasing chain of spans therefore has at most d(G)+1 strict steps. At an index s with (1, val_{sigma^s}|_C) in R_{s-1}, the argument inside thm:qm-eval applies verbatim with D the answers up to s-1: any consistent harmonic system agrees with the game's own on R_{s-1}, hence at the point (1, val_{sigma^s}|_C), hence its frozen operator has val_{sigma^s}|_C as a fixed point, hence (uniqueness) as its value, and its appeals there are the true ones.
results.verification: code_dir/runrank.py runs the least-index rule of thm:ladder on L_n and all-switches on B1 and B2_small, and at every non-rank-adding round recomputes from scratch a harmonic system consistent with the EARLIER answers only and compares its prediction of the value vector and of all 2|C| appeals with the truth, in exact arithmetic. L_3: 8 rounds, 4 rank-adding (= |C|+1), 4 predicted, 0 mispredicted. L_4: 16 rounds, 5 rank-adding, 11 predicted. L_5: 32 rounds, 6 rank-adding, 26 predicted. L_6: 64 rounds, 7 rank-adding, 57 predicted. B1 all-switches: 1 round. B2_small all-switches: 5 rounds, 4 rank-adding, 1 predicted. Total mispredictions: 0.

results.name: Values beat orientations: a strict separation of the evaluation and outmap oracles
results.statement: There is a family S of stopping SSGs with four Max vertices and at most one Min vertex, on at most 152 vertices, with evaluation-query complexity 1 and deterministic outmap-query complexity 4. The ingredient is that the deterministic outmap-query complexity of the class of ALL acyclic unique sink orientations of the 3-cube — every one of which is realised by a stopping SSG with three Max vertices and at most one Min vertex — is exactly 4, while by thm:qm-eval no class ever costs more than |C|+2 evaluations.
results.why_not_implied: prop:allsw-auso identifies an all-switches run with a bottom-antipodal walk of the improvement orientation; it neither compares the information in the orientation with the information in the values nor produces any query count, and the exact number 4 for the 3-cube class is a new computation about a model the paper does not define.
results.argument: By prop:m3-realised and prop:m3-one-min every one of the eighteen AUSO classes of the 3-cube is the improvement orientation of a nondegenerate stopping SSG with three Max vertices and at most one Min vertex; realisability is invariant under renaming Max vertices and under swapping one Max vertex's two successors, and the orbits of the eighteen classes under the resulting group of order 48 are exactly the 728 AUSOs. Given such a G_s with sink z, let SEP(s) adjoin a DISJOINT Max vertex u whose action 0 enters a chain of five average vertices of value theta(z) = (2 idx(z)+1)/32 and whose action 1 enters h -> (t1,t0) of value 1/2. The two parts do not interact, so val_sigma splits, the improvement orientation is the product of s with the 1-cube combed towards action 1, and the sink is (1,z). One evaluation returns val_sigma(u^(0)) = theta(z), from which z is read off: Q(S) = 1. An outmap query at (b,sigma) returns s(sigma) u {u if b = 0}, so an outmap algorithm for S is an outmap algorithm for the whole 3-cube AUSO class, whence Q_out(S) >= 4; and 4 suffices. The separation is honest but cheap — the family broadcasts its own solution in a value. The substantial statement is thm:qm-eval: since Q <= |C|+2 always, ANY class on which the outmap oracle provably needs more than |C|+2 queries separates the two oracles by that margin, and no such class is known.
results.verification: code_dir/outmap_qc.py enumerates the orientations of the m-cube by backtracking: 2/2, 12/12, 744/728 USOs/AUSOs for m = 1,2,3, matching prop:auso-census exactly; its exact minimax decision-tree computation gives deterministic outmap-query complexity 1, 2, 4 for the AUSO classes, and an independent memo-free recursion (dout_check.py, written separately) gives the same 1, 2, 4. code_dir/m3check.py reloads the eighteen realisations from /data/ssg-proof/scripts/round16-verify/m3games, recomputes each improvement outmap FROM THE GAME (componentwise minimum over Min strategies of exact profile values), finds all eighteen stopping, nondegenerate and matching the stored outmap, and verifies that the orbit of the eighteen under the 48-element symmetry group is exactly the set of 728 AUSOs. code_dir/sep.py builds SEP(s) for a base game whose sink is moved to each of the eight corners by swapping successors and verifies, in exact arithmetic and for all eight: stopping, no tied incidence, orientation equal to the product of s with the combed 1-cube, sink (1,z), and theta decoded from a single evaluation equal to z. Logs: verify_E.log.

restatements.label: lem:readout
restatements.note: My lem:qm-form(b) — pinning ALL controlled vertices and reading off y(v^(a)) = q + p.y|_C — is lem:readout(a),(b) with C in place of Vmax, where the minimum over Min strategies disappears because Min is pinned too; the paper already uses these rows under the name harmonic normal form (lem:rise-bound, thm:lasserre-vacuous), so only its use, not its content, is new.

restatements.label: lem:survival-contract
restatements.note: My lem:qm-form(c) — a substochastic family of first-passage rows over C with no full-mass trapped set has a unique fixed point for max/min selections — is literally lem:survival-contract, whose statement already says 'the argument applies verbatim to any finite family of substochastic first-passage rows over C'; I reproved it only to make def:qm-harmonic self-contained for hypotheses that are not games.

restatements.label: prop:auso-census
restatements.note: My independent backtracking enumeration reproduced 12/12, 744/728 USOs/AUSOs of the 2- and 3-cube and the eighteen classes; that is a recount of prop:auso-census and is reported only as a check on the code that computes D_out.

restatements.label: lem:local-global
restatements.note: The observation that an answer with S_sigma empty is a free, checkable optimality certificate is lem:local-global; it is used, not restated as new.

gap: Whether the deterministic outmap-query complexity of the SSG-realisable orientations is superlinear — exactly: whether there is a constant c > 0 such that for infinitely many m there is a set R of acyclic unique sink orientations of the m-cube, each of them the improvement orientation of a stopping SSG on poly(m) vertices, on which every deterministic algorithm that sees only S_sigma needs at least m^{1+c} queries to name the sink.
next_steps: (1) Close the additive gap in cor:qm-theta: the evaluation-query complexity of one-player stopping SSGs with m Max vertices is between m and m+2, and the true value is unknown; a family forcing m+1 or m+2 would settle it, and the natural candidate is an HDP whose last bit is only certifiable by an extra query. (2) Attack the gap above: the realisable class at m = 3 is ALL 728 AUSOs and costs 4 outmap queries against 3 coordinates, so the outmap oracle is already superlinear-looking at the smallest size where the class is fully known; the next computable case is m = 4, where a certified realisable subclass is needed (the AP_m4_k0_* readout systems in the solo directory, plus disjoint unions of realised 3- and 1-cubes and of two 2-cubes, all realisable because the improvement orientation of a disjoint union is the product) — computing D_out over that set with a memory-bounded search would show whether D_out(4) exceeds 6 = |C|+2 and hence give a linear-against-superlinear separation instead of 1-against-4. (3) The decision version: HDP's members are pairwise isomorphic, so the threshold question is trivial there; whether the EVALUATION-query complexity of deciding val(v0) >= 1/2 (as opposed to naming an optimal strategy) is more than O(1) is open and is the honest remaining question in the model. (4) rem:qm-eval isolates a target-equivalent reformulation worth its own route: 'from evaluation data D, produce in polynomial time a strategy that is optimal for SOME stopping harmonic system consistent with D'; by thm:qm-eval such a rule solves SSG-Value, and by cor:qm-runs the data has less than full rank at all but |C|+1 rounds of any long run, so the relaxation is real everywhere except at the end. (5) The paper should record cor:qm-nobarrier next to rem:blowup-realise, since it fixes in advance what the blow-up programme can and cannot deliver.
prior_art: From memory, UNCHECKED against sources. (i) The recovery step — identifying the rows of a transient Markov decision process from on-policy value vectors, and the 'optimism/equivalence-query' loop that follows (hypothesise a consistent model, solve it, test its optimum, repeat) — is the standard certainty-equivalence / model-identification scheme of reinforcement learning and of exact learning with equivalence queries; the specific consequence that |C|+1 evaluations determine a stopping SSG's first-passage rows may well be folklore there, and I claim novelty only relative to this paper. (ii) The query complexity of sink-finding on abstract cubes is Szabo–Welzl (deterministic O(1.61^m), the Fibonacci seesaw) and Schurr–Szabo (a deterministic lower bound of order m^2/log m), with Matousek and Matousek–Szabo for the randomised side; all of these are for GENERAL unique sink orientations, not for the realisable ones, and none of them is imported or used here — thm:qm-eval and thm:qm-hdp are proved from scratch, and the only number I computed in that world (D_out = 4 for the 3-cube) is my own exhaustive minimax. (iii) The adversary in thm:qm-hdp is the standard adversary for the string-guessing game with longest-correct-prefix feedback (a Mastermind-type feedback), and the log-branching entropy bound for its randomised version is Shannon's. (iv) The paper's own prior art is untouched: I use lem:trapchar, lem:local-global, thm:contraction, lem:survival-contract, lem:readout, prop:m3-realised, prop:m3-one-min, prop:auso-census, and no fifth external theorem.

\subsection{The strategy-evaluation oracle: how many evaluations a game costs}\label{sec:qm}

Every rule in this paper interrogates its game in exactly one way: it
evaluates a positional strategy.  All-switches, \Cref{def:bsi},
$R_{\mathrm{BR}}$, the least-index rule of \Cref{thm:ladder}, the
one-player bias homotopy of \Cref{sec:bias} and the random facet of
\Cref{def:rf} all consist of a sequence of evaluations together with a
recipe for choosing the next strategy from the ones already evaluated.
This subsection takes the number of evaluations as the cost and asks what
it is.  The answer is $\Theta(|C|)$, both halves proved: at most
$|C|+2$ evaluations always suffice (\Cref{thm:qm-eval}) and $|\Vmax|$ are
sometimes necessary (\Cref{thm:qm-hdp}).  The consequence for this paper
is negative and sharp: none of its exponential lower bounds --- and none
that a family of exponential bottom-antipodal height would add --- is an
obstruction to an algorithm that is allowed to choose which strategies to
evaluate.  They are all bounds on the number of rounds of a fixed rule.

\begin{definition}[The controlled skeleton and the evaluation oracle]\label{def:qm-oracle}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG and $C:=\Vmax\cup\Vmin$, $c:=|C|$.  The
\emph{controlled skeleton} of $G$ is
$\Sigma(G):=\bigl(C,\ \mathrm{owner},\ (v^{(0)},v^{(1)})_{v\in C}\bigr)$:
the controlled vertices, the owner of each, and the \emph{names} of the two
successors of each, with the information of which of those names coincide
and which are sinks.  It says nothing whatever about $\Vavg$.  The
\emph{evaluation oracle} of $G$ answers a query $\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{\Vmax}$
with
\[
  \mathcal O_G(\sigma)\ :=\
  \bigl(\val_\sigma(u)\bigr)_{u\in C\,\cup\,\{v^{(a)}\;:\;v\in C,\ a\in\{0,1\}\}},
\]
the values, under $\sigma$ and an optimal Min reply, of the controlled
vertices and of everything they read.  An \emph{evaluation algorithm} is
given $\Sigma(G)$, queries the oracle adaptively, and must output an
optimal Max strategy.  For a class $\mathcal G$ of stopping games,
$Q(\mathcal G)$ denotes the least $q$ for which some deterministic
evaluation algorithm is correct on every $G\in\mathcal G$ using at most
$q$ queries.  The \emph{outmap oracle} $\mathcal O^{\mathrm{out}}_G$ is
the weaker one returning only $S_\sigma$, and $Q^{\mathrm{out}}$ its
complexity.
\end{definition}

Three remarks fix the model.  \emph{First}, one query is a polynomial-time
operation (\Cref{thm:eval-stopfree}), so $Q$ measures the shape of an
algorithm and not a concealed call to the problem itself; this is what
separates \Cref{def:qm-oracle} from the \textsc{SSG-Compare} oracle of
\Cref{thm:compare-equivalence}, where $n$ non-adaptive calls suffice for
the trivial reason that one call is already as hard as the game.
\emph{Second}, the halting test is free: an answer with $S_\sigma=\emptyset$
certifies optimality by \Cref{lem:local-global}, so a correct algorithm may
always stop with a proof, and $Q$ is unchanged if we demand one.
\emph{Third}, an evaluation algorithm is not required to run in polynomial
time between queries, and the one built below does not; \Cref{thm:qm-eval}
is a statement about information, and says nothing about
\textsc{SSG-Value} being in \textsf{P}.

\begin{definition}[Harmonic systems]\label{def:qm-harmonic}
A \emph{harmonic system} on a finite owner-labelled set $C$ is a family of
rows $\rho_{v,a}=(q_{v,a},p_{v,a})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{C}$,
$v\in C$, $a\in\{0,1\}$, with $q_{v,a}+|p_{v,a}|_1\le1$, subject to the
\emph{stopping condition}: there is no nonempty $U\subseteq C$ such that
every $v\in U$ has an action $a$ with $q_{v,a}=0$, $|p_{v,a}|_1=1$ and
$\operatorname{supp}p_{v,a}\subseteq U$.  Its operators are
$(T_\rho y)_v:=\operatorname{opt}_a(q_{v,a}+p_{v,a}\cdot y)$ on $\mathbb R^{C}$,
$\max$ at Max and $\min$ at Min, and $T_{\rho,\sigma}$, $T_{\rho,\sigma,\tau}$
with the indicated players frozen.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The harmonic form of a game]\label{lem:qm-form}
Let $G$ be stopping and let $\rho_{v,a}$ be the first-passage law of the
action $a$ at $v$ onto $C\cup\{t_1\}$ --- $p_w$ the probability that the
token, leaving $v$ by $a$, next meets a controlled vertex at $w$, and $q$
that it reaches $t_1$ first; the harmonic normal form used at
\Cref{lem:rise-bound} and \Cref{thm:lasserre-vacuous}.  Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $\rho$ is a harmonic system;
\item if $y\in[0,1]^{V}$ is the mean of its two successors at every average
      vertex, with $y(t_0)=0$ and $y(t_1)=1$, then
      $y(v^{(a)})=q_{v,a}+p_{v,a}\cdot y|_{C}$ for all $v\in C,a\in\{0,1\}$.
      In particular $\val_{\sigma,\tau}|_C$ is a fixed point of
      $T_{\rho,\sigma,\tau}$, $\val_\sigma|_C$ one of $T_{\rho,\sigma}$, and
      $w^\ast|_C$ one of $T_\rho$;
\item every operator of a harmonic system has exactly one fixed point.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(a) Absorption in $C\cup\{t_0,t_1\}$ is almost sure from every vertex:
a trajectory that stayed in $\Vavg$ for ever would never reach a sink,
which has probability $0$ under every positional pair since $G$ is
stopping.  So $\rho_{v,a}$ is a substochastic law.  For the stopping
condition let $U\ne\emptyset$ be as excluded and pick at each $v\in U$ a
full-mass action $a(v)$.  Leaving $v$ by $a(v)$ the token meets
$C\cup\{t_0,t_1\}$ inside $U$ almost surely, so no average vertex $u$ on
the way can have a sink among its successors (that would give a positive
probability of a sink first), and every successor of such a $u$ is again
either such an average vertex or a member of $U$.  Hence $U$ together with
those average vertices is a nonempty trap, against \Cref{lem:trapchar}.

(b) Let $H$ be the hitting time of $C\cup\{t_0,t_1\}$ by the token started
at $v^{(a)}$ and moving by fair coins at average vertices ($H=0$ if
$v^{(a)}$ already lies there).  By the previous paragraph $H<\infty$ a.s.;
$y$ is bounded and $(y(X_{k\wedge H}))_k$ is a martingale because $y$ is
the mean of its successors at every average vertex; optional stopping gives
$y(v^{(a)})=\mathbb E\,y(X_H)=q_{v,a}+p_{v,a}\cdot y|_C$.  Each
$\val_{\sigma,\tau}$, $\val_\sigma$ and $w^\ast$ satisfies the average
equations and the sink pinning, and equals, at a controlled vertex, the
frozen resp.\ optimised choice among its two successors' values.

(c) Let $(S\xi)_v:=\max_a p_{v,a}\cdot\xi$ on $\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{C}$.
$S^{n}\bbone$ decreases to a fixed point $\xi$ of $S$.  If
$\mu:=\max\xi>0$ then for $v\in U:=\{\xi=\mu\}$ some action has
$p_{v,a}\cdot\xi=\mu$; since $\xi\le\mu$ and $p\ge0$ this forces
$|p_{v,a}|_1=1$, hence $q_{v,a}=0$, and equality forces
$\operatorname{supp}p_{v,a}\subseteq U$ --- the configuration excluded by
\Cref{def:qm-harmonic}.  So $S^{n}\bbone\to0$, and for some $n$,
$\lVert S^{n}\bbone\rVert_\infty\le\frac12$.  As
$|\operatorname{opt}_aA_a-\operatorname{opt}_aB_a|\le\max_a|A_a-B_a|$ we get
$|T_\rho^{n}y-T_\rho^{n}y'|\le S^{n}|y-y'|$ pointwise, so $T_\rho^{n}$ is a
sup-norm contraction; the same domination holds for the frozen operators.
This is the argument of \Cref{lem:survival-contract}, which states it for
an arbitrary finite family of substochastic first-passage rows over $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Evaluation dimension]\label{def:qm-dim}
For a stopping SSG $G$ put
$\mathcal V(G):=\{\val_\sigma|_C\;:\;\sigma\in\{0,1\}^{\Vmax}\}\subseteq[0,1]^{C}$
and $d(G):=\dim\operatorname{aff}\mathcal V(G)\le|C|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation is cheap]\label{thm:qm-eval}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG.  The following deterministic evaluation
algorithm outputs an optimal Max strategy of $G$, together with a
certificate of optimality, after at most $d(G)+2\le|C|+2$ queries.
\begin{quote}
\textsc{Algorithm E}.  Keep the list $D$ of answers received, an answer
being a pair $(x,A)$ with $x=\val_\sigma|_C$ and $A(v,a)=\val_\sigma(v^{(a)})$.
Choose a harmonic system $\hat\rho$ on $\Sigma(G)$ \emph{consistent with
$D$}, i.e.\ with $\hat q_{v,a}+\hat p_{v,a}\cdot x=A(v,a)$ for every
$(x,A)\in D$ and every $(v,a)$; let $\hat w$ be the fixed point of
$T_{\hat\rho}$ and $\hat\sigma$ a Max-greedy strategy at $\hat w$; query
$\hat\sigma$.  If the answer has $S_{\hat\sigma}=\emptyset$, output
$\hat\sigma$; otherwise append it to $D$ and repeat.
\end{quote}
Consequently $Q(\mathcal G)\le c+2$ for every class $\mathcal G$ of
stopping SSGs with $|C|\le c$; since $|C|\le N-2$ this is $Q\le N$ always.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Well defined.}  By \Cref{lem:qm-form}(a),(b) the harmonic form
$\rho_G$ of $G$ is a harmonic system consistent with $D$ at every stage, so
the choice is from a nonempty set.  By \Cref{lem:qm-form}(c) the fixed
point $\hat w$ exists and is unique; if $\hat\sigma$ is Max-greedy at
$\hat w$ then $T_{\hat\rho,\hat\sigma}\hat w=\hat w$, so $\hat w$ is
\emph{the} value of $\hat\sigma$ in the hypothesis and no Max vertex is
strictly switchable at $\hat\sigma$ there.

\emph{Correct.}  The halting test is applied to the true answer, so it
says that no Max vertex of $G$ is strictly switchable at $\hat\sigma$;
by \Cref{lem:local-global}, $\val_{\hat\sigma}=w^\ast$.

\emph{At most $d(G)+1$ non-halting queries.}  Write
$u(x):=(1,x)\in\mathbb R^{1+C}$ and let $V_t:=\operatorname{span}\{u(x):(x,A)\in D\}$
after $t$ answers have been recorded.  Consistency with $D$ says exactly
that $\hat\rho_{v,a}-\rho_{G,v,a}\perp u(x)$ for every recorded $x$, hence
$\hat\rho_{v,a}-\rho_{G,v,a}\perp V_t$ for all $(v,a)$.  Suppose the
$(t+1)$-st query $\hat\sigma$ does not halt, and let
$x:=\val_{\hat\sigma}|_C$ be the true answer's value part.  If
$u(x)\in V_t$ then for every $(v,a)$
\[
  \hat q_{v,a}+\hat p_{v,a}\cdot x
  \;=\;q_{v,a}+p_{v,a}\cdot x\;=\;\val_{\hat\sigma}(v^{(a)})
\]
by \Cref{lem:qm-form}(b); taking the frozen/optimised choice at each
controlled vertex, $x$ is a fixed point of $T_{\hat\rho,\hat\sigma}$, hence
by \Cref{lem:qm-form}(c) \emph{the} value of $\hat\sigma$ in the hypothesis,
and the displayed identity says that the hypothesis's appeals at
$\hat\sigma$ are the true ones.  So the hypothesis's strictly switchable
set at $\hat\sigma$ --- empty by construction --- is the true one, and the
query halts: a contradiction.  Hence $u(x)\notin V_t$ and
$\dim V_{t+1}=\dim V_t+1$.  Since $\dim V_0=0$ and every recorded $x$ lies
in $\mathcal V(G)$, whose points span an affine space of dimension $d(G)$,
we have $\dim V_t\le d(G)+1$ throughout, so there are at most $d(G)+1$
non-halting queries and at most $d(G)+2$ in all.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:qm-eval}
Three features of the proof deserve emphasis.  (i) It uses \emph{no}
property of the choice of $\hat\rho$ beyond consistency and the stopping
condition; any selection rule gives the same bound.  (ii) It never needs
the true rows: when $\dim V_t=|C|+1$ they are determined, but the algorithm
stops long before if it can.  (iii) The step it cannot perform in
polynomial time is solving the hypothesis --- which is an SSG-valued
problem on the same controlled set --- so \Cref{thm:qm-eval} is not a step
towards \textsc{(Poly-Rule)}.  Call $\sigma$ \emph{justified} by $D$ if some harmonic system
consistent with $D$ has $\sigma$ optimal.  The proof shows that a
polynomial-time rule producing a justified strategy from $D$ would put
\textsc{SSG-Value} in \textsf{P}; and the reformulation is
target-equivalent rather than a genuine simplification, because once
$\dim V_t=|C|+1$ the only consistent harmonic system is the game's own,
so the last justified strategy demanded is an optimal strategy of the
given game.  It is a relaxation only while the data has less than full
rank --- which is where all but $|C|+1$ of the rounds of any long run
sit (\Cref{cor:qm-runs}).
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[The profile oracle]\label{rem:qm-profile}
\Cref{thm:qm-eval} holds verbatim for the \emph{profile} oracle, which
takes a positional pair $(\sigma,\tau)$ and returns $\val_{\sigma,\tau}$ on
$C$ and on the successors of $C$ --- the cheapest evaluation there is, a
Markov chain.  Algorithm E is modified only in that $\hat\sigma$ is
replaced by a greedy \emph{pair} at $\hat w$ and the halting test asks that
no controlled vertex be strictly switchable, which by \Cref{lem:qm-form}(b)
makes $\val_{\sigma,\tau}$ a fixed point of the Shapley operator and hence
$w^\ast$ by \Cref{thm:contraction}.  The rank argument is unchanged.  So
the bidirectional rules of \Cref{def:bsi} and $R_{\mathrm{BR}}$, whose unit
of work is exactly a pair evaluation, also live in a model whose
information-theoretic cost is $|C|+2$.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[No evaluation-model barrier]\label{cor:qm-nobarrier}
No adversary argument in the model of \Cref{def:qm-oracle} can prove a
lower bound exceeding $|C|+2$.  In particular each of $L_n$
(\Cref{thm:ladder}), $H_m$ (\Cref{cor:slack-stalls}), $\mathrm{WD}(e,j,m)$
(\Cref{thm:wedge-proved}), $\mathrm{CC}(L,m)$ (\Cref{thm:hybrid-lower})
and $\mathrm{CV}(e,s)$ (\Cref{thm:cv-lower}) --- each of which defeats some
rule or calculus for $2^{\Omega(N)}$ rounds --- is solved by at most
$|C|+2$ evaluations, and a family of exponential bottom-antipodal height
realised on polynomially many vertices (\Cref{rem:blowup-realise}) would
defeat all-switches without being an informational obstacle: the same
instances would be solved by $|C|+2$ evaluations of the very operation
those rules perform once per round.  The subexponential bound of
\Cref{thm:subexp} is likewise a bound on a rule that follows improving
switches and reads only the orientation, not on the number of evaluations.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[A run stops informing after $|C|+1$ rounds]\label{cor:qm-runs}
Let $\sigma^{0},\sigma^{1},\dots$ be \emph{any} sequence of Max strategies
--- a run of any rule --- and let
$R_s:=\operatorname{span}\{(1,\val_{\sigma^{r}}|_C):r\le s\}$.  Then
$(1,\val_{\sigma^{s}}|_C)\notin R_{s-1}$ for at most $d(G)+1\le|C|+1$
indices $s$, and at every other index the value vector $\val_{\sigma^{s}}|_C$
\emph{and} all its appeals $\val_{\sigma^{s}}(v^{(a)})$ are already
determined: every harmonic system consistent with the answers at
$\sigma^{0},\dots,\sigma^{s-1}$ predicts them exactly, by the argument of
\Cref{thm:qm-eval}.  An exponentially long run therefore spends all but at
most $|C|+1$ of its rounds recomputing consequences of what its first few
evaluations already implied.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}[The hidden decision path]\label{def:qm-hdp}
For $m\ge1$ and $z\in\{0,1\}^{m}$ let $\mathrm{HDP}_m(z)$ be the one-player
stopping SSG on $6m$ non-sink vertices with $\Vmax=\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}$
built as follows.  Vertex $v_j$ owns the block
$e^{j}_0,e^{j}_1,x_j,y_j,s_j$ of five average vertices and points at
$(e^{j}_0,e^{j}_1)$ --- \emph{the same for every $z$}.  Write
$b_j:=e^{j}_{z_j}$ and $c_j:=e^{j}_{1-z_j}$.  For $j=1$:
$b_1\to(t_1,t_0)$, of value $\tfrac12$, and $c_1\to(t_0,x_1)$,
$x_1\to(t_1,t_0)$, of value $\tfrac14$ (the two remaining vertices of the
block are unreachable padding, wired $\to(t_0,t_0)$, and are present only
so that the layout does not depend on $z$).  For $j\ge2$:
$b_j\to(v_{j-1},x_j)$, $x_j\to(t_0,y_j)$, $y_j\to(t_1,t_0)$, whose
first-passage law onto $C\cup\{t_1\}$ is $(\tfrac18;\tfrac12\,e_{v_{j-1}})$,
and $c_j\to(t_0,s_j)$, $s_j\to(t_1,t_0)$, of value $\tfrac14$.  All
$2^{m}$ members have literally the same vertex kinds and the same
successor map on $C$, hence the same controlled skeleton; only the wiring
inside the gadgets, which $\Sigma(G)$ does not see, depends on $z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation is not free]\label{thm:qm-hdp}
Fix $m$ and let $\mathcal H_m:=\{\mathrm{HDP}_m(z):z\in\{0,1\}^m\}$.  Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item every $\mathrm{HDP}_m(z)$ is stopping, all $2^{m}$ members have the
      same controlled skeleton, and $\Opt(\mathrm{HDP}_m(z))=\{z\}$;
\item writing $i(\sigma,z):=\min\{j:\sigma_j\ne z_j\}$ (and $m+1$ if there
      is none), the value part of the oracle's answer is
      $x_j=\tfrac14+2^{-j-1}$ for $j<i$ and $x_j=\tfrac14$ for $j\ge i$;
      the appeals at $v_1$ are $\tfrac12$ against $\tfrac14$, and at $v_j$,
      $j\ge2$, are $\tfrac18+x_{j-1}/2$ against $\tfrac14$, so that
      $S_\sigma=\{v_i\}$ for $i\le m$ and $S_\sigma=\emptyset$ for $i=m+1$;
      consequently $\mathcal O(\sigma)$ depends on $z$ only through
      $z_1,\dots,z_{i(\sigma,z)}$, and reveals exactly those bits;
\item $Q(\mathcal H_m)=m$; and every randomised evaluation algorithm that
      is correct with probability $1$ makes at least $m/\log_2(m+1)$
      queries in expectation on a uniformly random member.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(a) Stopping: the trap test of \Cref{lem:trapchar} deletes first $y_j$ and
$s_j$, which have $t_0$ among their successors, then $x_j$ and $c_j$, which
have $t_0$ and a deleted vertex, then $b_j$, then every $v_j$, which now has
no successor left.  The skeleton is
$m$ Max vertices with $2m$ pairwise distinct successor names, none a sink
and none controlled, for every $z$: only which name is action $0$ changes,
and a name carries no other information.
(b) By \Cref{lem:qm-form}(b) the value restriction $x$ is the unique fixed
point of $x_j=\Psi_{j,\sigma_j}(x)$ where $\Psi_{j,z_j}(x)=\tfrac18+x_{j-1}/2$
($=\tfrac12$ for $j=1$) and $\Psi_{j,1-z_j}=\tfrac14$.  If $\sigma_j\ne z_j$
then $x_j=\tfrac14$; if $\sigma_j=z_j$ and $x_{j-1}=\tfrac14$ then
$x_j=\tfrac18+\tfrac18=\tfrac14$; and if $x_{j-1}=\tfrac14+2^{-j}$ then
$x_j=\tfrac14+2^{-j-1}$.  Induction on $j$ gives the displayed $x$, whence
the appeals: at $v_j$ with $j<i$ the pair is
$(\tfrac14+2^{-j-1},\tfrac14)$ with the first chosen, at $j=i$ the same
pair with the second chosen --- so $v_i$ is strictly switchable --- and at
$j>i$ the pair is $(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)$, a tie.  The answer is therefore
determined by $\sigma$ and $i$; and it determines $i$, hence
$z_1,\dots,z_{i-1}=\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{i-1}$ and $z_i=1-\sigma_i$, and
says nothing else.  $\Opt=\{z\}$ because $S_z=\emptyset$ and $S_\sigma\ne\emptyset$
for $\sigma\ne z$.
(c) \emph{Upper bound.}  Query $\sigma^1:=(0,\dots,0)$; the answer gives
$i_1$ and the bits $z_1..z_{i_1}$; query $\sigma^2$ agreeing with the known
prefix and $0$ elsewhere, and so on.  Each query enlarges the known prefix
by at least one bit, so after at most $m$ queries the whole of $z$ is known
and is output (and the algorithm stops earlier if some answer has
$S_\sigma=\emptyset$).
\emph{Lower bound.}  Let an algorithm be given.  The adversary keeps a
prefix $p$, initially empty.  On a query $\sigma$ it puts
$i:=\min\{j\le|p|:\sigma_j\ne p_j\}$ if that set is nonempty, and otherwise
$i:=|p|+1$ and extends $p$ by the bit $1-\sigma_{|p|+1}$; it answers with
the (unique, by (b)) answer belonging to $\sigma$ and $i$.  Every $z$
extending $p$ is consistent with all answers given so far, since
$z_j=p_j$ for $j\le|p|$ makes $i(\sigma^s,z)=i_s$ for each past query.
After $q$ queries $|p|\le q$; if $q\le m-1$ at least two extensions remain
and they have different optima by (a), so an output now is wrong for one of
them.  \emph{Randomised.}  Fix the random string: the algorithm becomes a
deterministic decision tree whose branching is at most $m+1$ (the answer is
a function of $\sigma$ and $i\in\{1,\dots,m+1\}$) and which must have at
least $2^{m}$ leaves, one per $z$.  A tree with branching $\le b$ and
$L$ leaves has average leaf depth at least $\log_b L$, so the expected
number of queries under the uniform $z$ is at least $m/\log_2(m+1)$;
averaging over the random string preserves the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The cost of a game is linear in its controlled set]\label{cor:qm-theta}
$|\Vmax|\le Q\le|C|+2$ over the stopping SSGs with a given controlled set,
already for one player: the evaluation-query complexity of finding an
optimal strategy is $\Theta(|C|)$, and the two bounds differ by at most an
additive $2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}[Values beat orientations]\label{prop:qm-separation}
There is a family $\mathcal S$ of stopping SSGs with four Max vertices and
at most one Min vertex, on at most $152$ vertices, with
$Q(\mathcal S)=1$ and $Q^{\mathrm{out}}(\mathcal S)=4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Every acyclic unique sink orientation of the $3$-cube is the improvement
orientation of a nondegenerate stopping SSG with three Max vertices and at
most one Min vertex: \Cref{prop:m3-realised} and \Cref{prop:m3-one-min}
supply one game per class, and realisability is invariant under the two
generators of the symmetry group --- renaming Max vertices, and swapping
the two successors of one Max vertex --- whose orbits of the eighteen
classes are the $728$ orientations.  For such a game $G_s$ with sink
$z\in\{0,1\}^{3}$ let $\mathrm{SEP}(s)$ adjoin a disjoint Max vertex $u$
whose action $0$ enters a chain of five average vertices of value
$\theta(z):=(2\,\mathrm{idx}(z)+1)/32$ and whose action $1$ enters
$h\to(t_1,t_0)$.  The two parts do not interact, so
$\val_\sigma$ splits and the improvement orientation of $\mathrm{SEP}(s)$
is the product of $s$ with the $1$-cube combed towards action $1$; its
sink is $(1,z)$.  One evaluation returns $\val_\sigma(u^{(0)})=\theta(z)$,
from which $z$ is read off, so $Q(\mathcal S)=1$.  An outmap query at
$(b,\sigma)$ returns $s(\sigma)\cup\{u\ \text{if}\ b=0\}$, so an outmap
algorithm for $\mathcal S$ is an outmap algorithm for the class of all
AUSOs of the $3$-cube, whose deterministic query complexity is $4$
(exhaustive minimax, below).  Hence $Q^{\mathrm{out}}(\mathcal S)\ge4$, and
$4$ suffices.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:qm-separation}
\Cref{prop:qm-separation} is the exact answer to ``is the value oracle
stronger than the orientation?''\ and it is a cheap one: the family
broadcasts its own solution in a value.  The substantial half is
\Cref{thm:qm-eval}: since $Q\le|C|+2$ unconditionally, \emph{any} class on
which the outmap oracle provably needs more than $|C|+2$ queries separates
the two by that margin, and none is known --- for the realisable
orientations the outmap-query complexity is not known to be superlinear.
What \Cref{cor:qm-nobarrier} does settle is that the abstraction of
\Cref{prop:allsw-auso} --- passing from the game to its improvement
orientation --- is exactly where the exponential lower bounds of this paper
live.  Discarding the numbers is not a harmless simplification: it is the
whole source of the difficulty in the cube picture.
\end{remark}
